notes.title: Enums as a type-safe, behavior-bearing domain model
objectives: Replace unrelated numeric or string flags with domain enum types
Choose fields, per-constant polymorphism or a mandatory strategy for varying behavior
Distinguish identifier name, presentation string and external stable code
notes.synthesis: An enum is an instance-controlled reference type with a fixed declaration set. The domain type prevents cross-domain values at compilation and can carry immutable data and methods. Constant-specific implementations force deliberate implementation of abstract behavior; a nested strategy enum can make policy selection mandatory without repeating implementations.
nuances: Enum constructors execute before normal static fields are initialized; build reverse lookup maps in later static initialization, not by registering in constant constructors.
values() follows declaration order; using its position as persistence or protocol identity is unsafe.
Changing a constant name can break name-based deserialization and Enum.valueOf; custom toString is a presentation mechanism, not an alternate identifier.
A strategy enum can prevent the silent default branch bug when a new constant uses an existing policy.
mistakes: Mixing transaction status int constants from separate domains
Using default switch behavior as a silent policy fallback
Persisting enum ordinal in a database
Using toString() output as the implicit wire key
notes.version: Core behavior available since Java 5; Java 21 exhaustive switch expressions can improve missing-case detection, but evolving an enum across separately compiled code still needs compatibility tests.
notes.interview: Refactor a payment state machine: typed state transitions, unknown external inputs, wire-code stability and safe addition of a state.
notes.demo: A renewal status adds SUSPENDED; the old default strategy silently treats it as APPROVED. Redesign to require an explicit state-specific policy.

notes.title: Keep domain codes and counts independent of enum ordinal
objectives: Separate declaration order from a persistent domain value
Support duplicate domain values and sparse codes
notes.synthesis: ordinal() represents declaration position for enum infrastructure, not business meaning. An explicit final field makes mapping stable under enum reordering and permits more than one constant to share a property or leave gaps.
nuances: An explicit code alone is not a complete compatibility plan: changing it also breaks persisted consumers.
EnumMap/EnumSet may use internal ordinals; application logic should not mimic their private implementation.
mistakes: Saving ordinal in a table then reordering declarations
Assuming sparse identifiers require dummy enum members
notes.version: Same rule on Java 5 through Java 21.
notes.interview: Migrate legacy integer statuses without changing historical rows; make unknown codes explicit.

notes.title: Model enum combinations with EnumSet
objectives: Express permission combinations without int masks
Understand mutability and generic Set-facing API design
notes.synthesis: EnumSet is an efficient typed set of constants from exactly one enum class. It supports normal set operations while avoiding arbitrary bit-width and cross-domain flag errors. Public APIs can accept Set<E> and use EnumSet internally.
nuances: EnumSet is mutable. Collections.unmodifiableSet returns an unmodifiable view, not a defensive snapshot; copy before wrapping if callers may retain and mutate source.
EnumSet.noneOf(Class<E>) is useful for an empty set with a known element type; EnumSet.copyOf an empty non-EnumSet collection cannot infer that element type.
No arbitrary 32/64 flag width limitation in the API; physical representation differs for larger enum types.
mistakes: Checking bit mask values as if they were strongly typed permissions
Sharing a mutable EnumSet across request boundaries
Treating unmodifiable views as immutable snapshots
notes.version: Java 21 retains mutable EnumSet; do not treat the book’s Java 9 forward-looking note about native immutable EnumSet as a guaranteed later feature.
notes.interview: Audit permissions parser and thread safety for a role-based access policy.
notes.demo: Authorization flags accumulate through shared mutable EnumSet exposed by a configuration cache.

notes.title: Index enum-keyed data with EnumMap instead of ordinals
objectives: Replace parallel ordinal-indexed arrays and unsafe casts
Model single and nested enum-keyed lookups
Choose explicit semantics for missing entries
notes.synthesis: EnumMap maps a known enum key type to values while hiding ordinal-indexed implementation details. For a pair of enum dimensions, use nested EnumMap where appropriate. This avoids handwritten offsets, unsafe generic-array casts and fragile declaration-order coupling.
nuances: Collectors.groupingBy without a supplied map factory does not promise EnumMap; a three-argument collector can select EnumMap explicitly.
A grouping result may omit a key for which no rows exist; prepopulate the desired empty groups if consumers require total coverage.
An absent transition should have an explicit representation (e.g., Optional or a named result); do not blindly propagate null through state-machine logic.
EnumMap permits null values but not null keys; null means an unknown or invalid enum identity, not a valid map bucket.
mistakes: Using state.ordinal() as an array index
Assuming groupingBy yields all enum values
Confusing undefined transition with a defined no-op transition
notes.version: EnumMap and nested maps work on Java 21; Java 21 switch expressions may be preferable for small total state mappings with compiler-enforced cases.
notes.interview: Design a lifecycle-transition engine that makes forbidden transitions observable and safely expands to a fourth state.

notes.title: Extend enum-like operations through an interface contract
objectives: Explain why enum inheritance is disallowed
Build an interface implemented by separate enum families
Decide between bounded Class tokens and a flexible Collection of operations
notes.synthesis: An enum cannot extend another enum, but distinct enum types can implement a common behavior interface. APIs typed to the interface can accept new plugin operations. A bounded Class<T extends Enum<T> & Capability> supports traversing one enum family; a Collection<? extends Capability> supports mixing families.
nuances: An interface does not automatically provide a unified values() over all implementors.
EnumSet and EnumMap are restricted to a single concrete enum class; mixing plugin enum types requires another collection representation.
Separate enum implementations do not inherit common fields; use interface defaults or helper composition when justified.
A plugin API must handle trust and registration boundaries separately; adding an interface does not make arbitrary plugin execution safe.
mistakes: Trying enum Extended extends Base
Assuming all interface implementations can be gathered via Enum.values
Accepting one enum implementation type instead of contract in extensible API
notes.version: Works since Java 5; Java 21 sealed interfaces intentionally restrict implementations, so avoid sealing a truly extensible plugin contract.
notes.interview: Design a pluggable reconciliation rule set using third-party Enum implementations without altering the built-in enum.

notes.title: Annotations provide explicit metadata contracts, not name magic
objectives: Choose retention and target for framework-discovered metadata
Implement repeatable annotation discovery correctly
Validate reflection invocation shape and exception behavior
notes.synthesis: An explicit annotation expresses an intention that a naming prefix cannot enforce. A runtime scanner needs RUNTIME retention, suitable target restrictions and correct reflective checks. Repeating an annotation uses a container, so query with getAnnotationsByType rather than relying on isAnnotationPresent for both single and repeated forms.
nuances: A method annotation does not enforce zero parameters, static access or public visibility by itself; an engine must validate invocation constraints.
InvocationTargetException wraps failures from invoked methods; distinguish user exception from scanner misuse.
Repeatable annotation container retention and target must be compatible with the repeated annotation.
isAnnotationPresent on the repeatable type can miss a repeated instance stored inside its container.
A Class<? extends Throwable> parameter enforces a type bound at compile time, while the referenced class may still be absent at runtime.
mistakes: Collecting methods by name prefix
Forgetting RUNTIME retention
Relying on isAnnotationPresent alone for repeated annotations
Treating the existence of an annotation as a validated executable test
notes.version: Repeatable annotations exist since Java 8; on Java 21 getAnnotationsByType handles direct and contained repeatable annotations, and inherited behavior depends on target, @Inherited and reflection API.
notes.interview: Build a small annotation-driven job-discovery layer with precise failure reporting and safe boundaries.

notes.title: Use @Override as a compile-time intent check
objectives: Distinguish overload from override with compiler feedback
Apply @Override consistently to superclass and interface methods
notes.synthesis: @Override makes the compiler check that a declared instance method really overrides or implements a supertype declaration. This catches signature drift, especially accidental equals overloads and interface contract mismatches, before they become latent bugs.
nuances: An accidental equals(MyType) overload is not Object.equals(Object) and leaves collections using identity equality.
The annotation is legal for interface implementations; it is optional but helpful for concrete required abstract methods.
Static methods hide rather than override; private methods are not overridable.
@Override verifies the override relationship, not the correctness of the implementation or equals/hashCode contract.
mistakes: Writing equals(Transaction) while expecting HashSet de-duplication
Assuming override annotation provides semantic correctness
Suppressing compiler error by removing annotation rather than fixing signature
notes.version: Java 21 compiles @Override on interface implementation and default-method overrides; review modern record-generated methods separately when custom equals is introduced.
notes.interview: Identify a production deduplication bug caused by overload and explain what annotations would and would not catch.

notes.title: Marker interface versus marker annotation: compile-time type boundary
objectives: Choose a type-level capability marker when APIs need it as a parameter bound
Use an annotation for methods, fields or framework metadata
notes.synthesis: A marker interface has no methods but introduces a type the compiler can enforce as a parameter or generic bound. A marker annotation adds metadata without making the annotated object assignable to a Java interface. Select based on whether the API must restrict acceptable instance types or merely tag an element.
nuances: Serializable is a marker interface but ObjectOutputStream.writeObject accepts Object; the library API does not take advantage of the marker type to reject an invalid caller at compile time.
A marker interface can extend a particular parent interface to narrow the set of admissible implementations.
Marker annotations can target methods, packages or other program elements impossible to represent as implemented types.
An interface with no new methods can still refine inherited behavioral contracts, so empty does not automatically mean mere marker.
mistakes: Expecting a @Signed annotation to satisfy a method parameter of type Signed
Claiming marker interfaces are obsolete in an annotation-heavy ecosystem
Assuming Serializable prevents runtime serialization failures
notes.version: Java 21 sealed marker hierarchies can deliberately restrict membership; this is a domain design choice not part of Java 5-era marker semantics.
notes.interview: Define a trusted-delivery capability for a typed API, and separately a method-level audit annotation.
